## Sampling Distributions for Non-Normal RVs

We learned that if a collection of independent random variables $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n$ are normally distributed, then the sample mean is also normally distributed.

What if instead of being normally distributed, we have one of the following scenarios:

-   $X_i \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{Unif}(a, b)$
-   $X_i \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{Exp}(\lambda)$
-   $X_i \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{Gamma}(\alpha, \lambda)$
-   $X_i \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{Beta}(\alpha, \beta)$

Here $\overset{iid}{\sim}$ is a shortcut for saying the random variables are independent and identically distributed where identically distributed means they each have the same distribution with the same parameters.

## Central Limit Theorem

::: {.callout title="Theorem 18.1"}
If $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n$ are independent and identically distributed random variables with mean $\text{E}[X_i] = \mu$ and variance $\text{Var}[X_i] = \sigma^2 < \infty$, then as $n \rightarrow \infty$:

$$
\sqrt{n}(\bar{X} - \mu) \overset{D}{\rightarrow} N(0, \sigma)
$$

For sufficiently large $n$ this means that:

$$
\bar{X} \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N\left(\mu, \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \right)
$$
:::

Here $\overset{D}{\rightarrow}$ means converges in distribution and $\overset{\cdot}{\sim}$ means approximately distributed.

## Ex: Machine Life

::: {.callout title="Example 18.1"}
The amount of time (in hours) a machine can run before requiring maintenance follows a gamma distribution with shape parameter $\alpha = 10$ and rate parameter $\lambda = 2$. A company monitors the times of 50 different machines.

What is the approximate sampling distribution of $\bar{X}$ for the average lifetime of these 50 machines?
:::

. . .

According to the Central Limit Theorem we have the following:

$$
\begin{align}
\bar{X} & \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N\left(\frac{\alpha}{\lambda}, \sqrt{\frac{\alpha}{n\lambda^2}}\right) \\
& \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N\left(5, \sqrt{0.05}\right)
\end{align}
$$

## Ex: Screw Weights

::: {.callout title="Example 18.4"}
A factory produces screws, and the weight (in grams) of a screw is known to have a mean of 5.2 grams and a standard deviation of 0.8 grams. However, the exact distribution of screw weights is unknown.

If a random sample of 40 screws is taken, what is the approximate sampling distribution of the sample mean weight?
:::

. . .

According to the Central Limit Theorem, we have:

$$
\bar{X} \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N\left(5.2, \frac{0.8}{\sqrt{40}} \right)
$$

## Ex: Access Times

::: {.callout title="Example 18.5"}
A computer system’s memory access times (in nanoseconds) follow an unknown distribution with a mean of 100 ns and a standard deviation of 20 ns. You collect a random sample of 36 memory accesses.

If you collect a random sample of 36 memory access times, what is the approximate sampling distribution of the sample mean weight for these 36 observations?
:::

. . .

According to the Central Limit Theorem, we have:

$$
\bar{X} \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N\left(100, \frac{20}{\sqrt{36}} \right)
$$

## Computing Exact Probabilities for Gamma Means

::: {.callout title="Theorem 18.2"}
Let $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n$ be independent gamma random variables with shape $\alpha$ and rate $\lambda$. Then the following is true:

$$
P(\bar{X} \leq \bar{x}) = F_X(n\times\bar{x}; n \times \alpha, \lambda)
$$

where $F_X(n\times\bar{x}; n \times \alpha, \lambda)$ is the CDF for a gamma distribution with shape parameter $n \times \alpha$ and rate parameter $\lambda$.
:::

. . .

$$
\begin{align}
P(\bar{X} \leq \bar{x}) &= P\left(\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i \leq \bar{x}\right) \\
&= P\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \leq n\times\bar{x}\right) \\
&= F_X(n \times \bar{x}; n \times \alpha, \lambda) & \text{Since} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i \sim \text{Gamma}(n\times \alpha, \lambda)
\end{align}
$$

## Ex: Machine Life

::: {.callout title="Example 18.8"}
The amount of time (in hours) a machine can run before requiring maintenance follows a gamma distribution with shape parameter $\alpha = 10$ and rate parameter $\lambda = 2$. A company monitors the times of 50 different machines.

What is the probability that the average lifetime exceeds 5.5 hours?
:::

. . .

According to the Central Limit Theorem we have the following:

$$
\bar{X} \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N\left(5, \sqrt{0.05}\right)
$$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
mu_xbar <- 5
sigma_xbar <- sqrt(0.05)

1-pnorm(5.5, mu_xbar, sigma_xbar)
1-pgamma(50*5.5, 50*10, 2)
```

## Ex: Screw Weights

::: {.callout title="Example 18.11"}
A factory produces screws, and the weight (in grams) of a screw is known to have a mean of 5.2 grams and a standard deviation of 0.8 grams. However, the exact distribution of screw weights is unknown.

If a random sample of 40 screws is taken, what is the probability that the average weight of these 40 screws is less than 5 or greater than 5.4?
:::

. . .

According to the Central Limit Theorem, we have:

$$
\bar{X} \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N\left(5.2, \frac{0.8}{\sqrt{40}} \right)
$$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
mu_xbar <- 5.2
sigma_xbar <- 0.8/sqrt(40)
pnorm(5, mu_xbar, sigma_xbar) + (1-pnorm(5.4, mu_xbar, sigma_xbar))
2*pnorm(5, mu_xbar, sigma_xbar)
```

## Ex: Access Times

A computer system’s memory access times (in nanoseconds) follow an unknown distribution with a mean of 100 ns and a standard deviation of 20 ns.

If a random sample of 36 memory accesses is recorded, what is the probability that the average memory access time exceeds 105 ns?
:::

. . .

According to the Central Limit Theorem, we have:

$$
\bar{X} \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N\left(100, \frac{20}{\sqrt{36}} \right)
$$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
mu_xbar <- 100
sigma_xbar <- 20/sqrt(36)

1-pnorm(105, mu_xbar, sigma_xbar)
```
